cases.question: What did the observatory ultimately use to stop vibration from spoiling the night photographs?
cases.answer: A suspended tray filled with dry grains.

truth_claims.claim: A suspended tray filled with dry grains.

turns.content: The observatory vibration review tested rubber feet for night photographs, but rejected them after image shake remained.
Foam pads were proposed to stop observatory vibration spoiling night photographs; the proposal was not adopted.
A training exercise claimed steel braces would stop vibration in night photographs, but labels that answer fictional.
The observatory tried cork blocks beneath the camera; vibration still spoiled the night photographs.
A draft suggested water bladders for observatory vibration control, then withdrew the idea before night photography.
Spring feet appeared in an obsolete observatory plan for vibration-free night photographs and were never installed.
The night photograph checklist mentions silicone mounts only as a failed observatory vibration experiment.
A neighboring observatory uses concrete piers against vibration, but our night photographs did not adopt that design.
The observatory vibration mockup labels lead weights as the night photography solution, while its footer says placeholder.
Air cushions were evaluated for stopping vibration during night photographs and failed the observatory stability test.
A rejected purchase order named magnetic feet for the observatory night camera vibration problem.
The observatory considered a hanging cable to prevent vibration spoiling night photographs, but cancelled it as unsafe.
A classroom worksheet answers that wax blocks stop observatory vibration in night photographs; it is explicitly synthetic.
The old night photography manual recommended wooden shims for vibration, and the observatory retired that advice.
A simulation used hydraulic legs to stop observatory vibration, but no real night photographs used them.
The observatory vibration committee discussed woven straps for night photographs without approving them.
A vendor advertised ceramic sockets for vibration-free observatory night photographs; the claim was rejected.
The observatory log says felt layers did not stop vibration from blurring the night photographs.
A night photography rehearsal used counterweights against observatory vibration only for demonstration.
The observatory rejected resin anchors after vibration continued to spoil night photographs.
A retired memo called a granite slab the observatory answer to night photograph vibration, then marked it obsolete.
The observatory's night photograph vibration trial with rubber cords ended without adoption.
A software fixture displays copper springs as the current observatory vibration control for night photographs; it is test data.
The observatory ruled out pneumatic columns for night photography because vibration remained measurable.
A proposed sandbag wall around the observatory camera did not stop vibration in night photographs and was removed.
The observatory tested a floating platform for night photographs, but vibration performance failed acceptance.
A fictional incident drill says a gyroscope stopped observatory vibration from spoiling night photographs.
The observatory archive records that tuned dampers were considered for night photographs but never authorized.
The signed field record gives the final arrangement: A suspended tray filled with dry grains. It eliminated image shake during dark-sky exposures.
The cafeteria ordered new trays and grain containers; this note has no relation to imaging equipment.
